presentingComplaint: High fever with rigors, right loin pain and increasing confusion over 2 days, now cold and clammy.
history: Type 2 diabetic (HbA1c 9.1%) woman brought to the emergency department with 48 hours of high-grade fever, shaking chills, right-sided loin pain and dysuria with urinary frequency. Over the preceding 6 hours she became drowsy, passed very little urine and felt cold and sweaty. No prior urinary catheter and no recent hospitalisation, but she was treated 3 months ago for an E. coli urinary infection that grew an ESBL-producing organism, managed at that time with oral fosfomycin. No prior stone disease. Not pregnant (post-menopausal). No abdominal surgery, no jaundice, no cough or diarrhoea.
examination: Toxic, drowsy but rousable, peripherally cool with mottled knees and prolonged capillary refill (4 s). Marked right costovertebral-angle tenderness; no renal-angle mass. Abdomen soft with no guarding, Murphy negative, no organomegaly. Chest clear, heart sounds normal with no murmur. No rash, no calf tenderness.

labs.urinalysis: leucocyte esterase 3+, nitrites positive, >100 WBC/hpf, numerous bacteria

imaging: Point-of-care and formal renal ultrasound: bulky, oedematous right kidney with loss of corticomedullary differentiation; no hydronephrosis, no calculus and no perinephric collection or abscess. No obstruction requiring drainage.
microbiology: Two sets of blood cultures and a clean-catch urine culture sent before antibiotics. Urine Gram stain shows Gram-negative bacilli. At 36 h both blood cultures and urine grow Escherichia coli >10^5 CFU/mL; susceptibility confirms an ESBL producer (ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin resistant) but susceptible to meropenem, ertapenem, amikacin and nitrofurantoin.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute pyelonephritis with urosepsis / septic shock (obstruction excluded on imaging)
Ascending cholangitis (excluded - normal bilirubin, no RUQ pain, biliary tree normal)
Undifferentiated septic shock from another source
finalDiagnosis: Acute pyelonephritis (ESBL E. coli) complicated by septic shock with acute kidney injury and lactic acidosis
citations: IDSA — Acute Uncomplicated Cystitis and Pyelonephritis in Women — 2011
Surviving Sepsis Campaign — Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock — 2021
IDSA — Guidance on Treatment of ESBL, AmpC and CRE Infections — 2024
stewardship: This is urosepsis with septic shock in a patient with a documented ESBL E. coli within 90 days, so empiric therapy must reliably cover ESBL organisms: give IV meropenem 1 g 8-hourly (dose-adjusted for AKI) within the first hour after cultures, alongside Surviving Sepsis resuscitation (30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid, source assessment, noradrenaline titrated to MAP >=65 mmHg). A carbapenem rather than piperacillin-tazobactam is preferred in shock given the ESBL history. Because ultrasound excludes obstruction, no urgent drainage is required. Once cultures confirm a meropenem-susceptible ESBL E. coli and the patient stabilises, de-escalate: for pyelonephritis, IV ertapenem 1 g daily is a carbapenem-sparing consolidation, and oral step-down to nitrofurantoin is NOT appropriate for pyelonephritis (inadequate renal-parenchymal levels) - so complete 10-14 days with a carbapenem or, if a susceptible oral agent emerges, an appropriate directed agent. Review daily and stop when the source is controlled.
contraindications: Avoid empiric ceftriaxone or ciprofloxacin monotherapy given prior ESBL and resistance on susceptibilities
Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin are inadequate for pyelonephritis and are contraindicated in significant AKI/renal parenchymal infection
Avoid nephrotoxic contrast/NSAIDs during AKI; dose-adjust renally cleared agents
Aminoglycosides need caution and level monitoring in AKI
edgeCases: If ultrasound had shown hydronephrosis or an obstructing stone, urgent urological decompression (stent/nephrostomy) would take priority over antibiotics alone
Failure to defervesce or clinical worsening at 48-72 h should prompt CT to exclude emphysematous pyelonephritis or perinephric/renal abscess
In a prior-CRE patient the empiric choice would escalate beyond meropenem (e.g. ceftazidime-avibactam)
expectedMaiK: Septic shock from acute pyelonephritis in a diabetic with prior ESBL E. coli - resuscitate per Surviving Sepsis and start empiric carbapenem cover within the hour, then de-escalate on culture.
expectedNextQuestions: Any prior urinary tract infections, and were resistant (ESBL/MDR) organisms grown?
Any urinary catheter, stones, obstruction or recent urological procedure?
Antibiotic exposure or hospitalisation in the last 90 days?
Urine output over the last few hours and fluid intake?
expectedInvestigations: Two sets of blood cultures plus urine culture and sensitivity BEFORE antibiotics
Serum lactate, venous blood gas and repeat after resuscitation
Renal function, electrolytes, FBC, CRP/procalcitonin, coagulation and glucose
Renal tract ultrasound (urgent) to exclude obstruction/abscess; CT if not improving

investigations: Blood cultures x2 and urine culture with sensitivities before antibiotics
Serum lactate and venous blood gas
Renal function, FBC, CRP/procalcitonin, coagulation, glucose
Renal tract ultrasound to exclude obstruction/abscess

regressionAssertions: Engine identifies PYELONEPHRITIS as the leading diagnosis
Recognises septic shock (hypotension + lactate + vasopressor) and triggers Surviving Sepsis resuscitation
Empiric antibiotic covers ESBL (carbapenem) given prior ESBL history rather than ceftriaxone/ciprofloxacin
Recommends renal tract imaging to exclude obstruction before assuming uncomplicated course
Advises culture-directed de-escalation and does not step down to nitrofurantoin/fosfomycin for pyelonephritis
